passage: Anirban, before you buy that "eighty percent success rate" course, let your Dolma aunty tell you something from when I was nineteen, a student in Darjeeling. A shop near the college had a sign on a winter jacket: "Twenty percent off! Save big!" The shop across the road sold the identical jacket with a sign that said, "You pay eighty percent of the price." Same price, I checked later. I felt I'd won something at the first shop, and I'd have walked straight past the second. And at the canteen, the "ninety percent fat-free" cake sold out every day, while nobody touched the one labelled "contains ten percent fat". Same cake, Anirban. The words did the choosing.

qa.q: What did the first shop's sign say?
qa.a: It said, "Twenty percent off! Save big!"

qa.q: Why did young Dolma feel she'd won something at the first shop?
qa.a: The "twenty percent off" wording made the price feel like a gain, while the same price described as paying eighty percent sounded like a loss.

qa.q: What could Anirban check before buying the "eighty percent success rate" course?
qa.a: Anirban could flip it to "twenty percent don't succeed", ask what that means in real numbers, and compare it with other courses before paying.

qa.q: How might the shop with the "you pay eighty percent" sign fare with the same jacket?
qa.a: That shop would likely sell far fewer jackets, even at the same price, simply because its wording made the deal sound like a loss.

grounding: Shows a student pulled toward offers worded as savings or percent fat-free and put off by the same figures worded as a cost.

passage: Madhav had ten minutes before the electronics shop closed, and his phone battery was at three percent. He needed a laptop for college, and the salesman, Shankar, was talking fast. "This warranty covers ninety percent of repair costs, sir. Peace of mind!" Madhav nodded; it sounded great. Then, at the billing counter, the cashier read from the form: "So you understand you'll pay ten percent of every repair yourself, plus the warranty fee?" Madhav hesitated. Suddenly it sounded like a trap. Same warranty, same fee. He stood there with his card half out, the shutters rattling down, trying to decide which sentence was the true one.

qa.q: What did the cashier say Madhav would pay?
qa.a: The cashier said he would pay ten percent of every repair himself, plus the warranty fee.

qa.q: Why did the warranty suddenly sound like a trap to Madhav?
qa.a: The cashier described the same deal as a cost he would pay, and that loss wording made it feel worse than the salesman's "covers ninety percent".

qa.q: How could Madhav judge the warranty on its own merits?
qa.a: He could write both versions side by side, work out the actual rupee cost of a typical repair, and ask for a day to decide rather than choosing in a rush.

qa.q: How might Shankar see the cashier's wording?
qa.a: Shankar may feel annoyed, since the gain-worded pitch was working and the cashier's version made the same deal sound like a loss.

grounding: Shows a student drawn in by a warranty worded as a gain and put off by the same terms worded as a loss, under time pressure.

passage: On the Delhi metro, Rashmi saw an ad for an evening coding course: "Register early and SAVE ₹2,000!" She smiled and took a photo. That night her friend Yash forwarded the same course's email: "A late fee of ₹2,000 applies after 1 June." Rashmi frowned. "Ugh, they're charging a penalty? That's so greedy." Yash laughed. "Rashmi, it's the same two thousand. Same course, same date." She looked at the photo and the email side by side. One made her feel clever; the other made her feel cheated. "Why do I like one and hate the other?" she asked. "Because ads know you better than you do," Yash said.

qa.q: What did the email say applies after 1 June?
qa.a: A late fee of ₹2,000 applies after 1 June.

qa.q: Why did the email make Rashmi feel cheated?
qa.a: Rashmi felt annoyed because the email framed the same two thousand as a penalty she would lose, while the ad framed it as savings she would gain, and losses sting more.

qa.q: What could Rashmi do the next time an offer tugs at her?
qa.a: She could rewrite the offer the opposite way and in plain rupees, then decide whether the course is worth that price regardless of the wording.

qa.q: How might the course's advertisers see Rashmi's two reactions?
qa.a: The advertisers probably know that "save" attracts more people than "late fee", which is why the ad she saw first used the gain wording.

grounding: Shows a student attracted by an offer worded as savings and put off by the same amount worded as a late fee, as ads intend.

passage:
"Tushar, look at this," Omkar said, turning his laptop towards his brother. "Gym near college: 'Get eighty percent of your deposit back, anytime!' That's so fair. I'm signing up."
Tushar, lying on the lower bunk, didn't look up. "So if you leave, they keep twenty percent."
Omkar frowned. "What? No. Keep twenty percent? That's a rip-off. Forget it."
"Bhai, it's the same deal. I just said it the other way."
Omkar looked at the screen again, then at Tushar. "Why does 'get back' feel generous and 'they keep' feel like theft?"
"Because that's how they wrote it. Every banner does it. 'Save,' 'bonus,' 'free.' Try saying the deposit in rupees."
Omkar did the maths. "Two thousand deposit. I'd lose four hundred if I quit."
"Now decide," Tushar said, finally sitting up. "Would you still go three times a week?"

qa.q: What did the gym's offer promise, in its own words?
qa.a: 'Get eighty percent of your deposit back, anytime!'

qa.q: Why did Omkar feel the same deal was fair one minute and a rip-off the next?
qa.a: Hearing 'get back' made him think about what he would gain, while 'they keep' made him think about losing money, and losses feel much worse even when the numbers match.

qa.q: What choice did Tushar push Omkar towards before signing up?
qa.a: He asked Omkar to put the deposit in rupees and then ask whether he would really go three times a week, so the decision rests on the plain cost and his own habits.

qa.q: How might Tushar see the gym's wording, compared with Omkar?
qa.a: Tushar seems used to spotting it, noticing that every banner uses words like 'save' and 'free', so for Tushar the wording is a tactic rather than a reason to buy.

grounding: It shows a student drawn in by an offer framed as a gain and put off by the identical offer framed as a loss, with ads relying on this.

passage:
I'm Disha, and I only understood this about packaging last month, in my second year of college. Mehak and I were in the corner shop after class, both thirsty. I picked up a juice carton that said in huge green letters: "90% real fruit!" I felt healthy just holding it.
Mehak reached for a cheaper carton on the lower shelf. On the back it said: "Contains 10% added syrup." I made a face and told her to put it down. Then she turned my carton around. Same small print. Same ten percent. Same company, even.
I stood there feeling a bit silly. The number hadn't changed, only which part they showed me first. Now I catch it everywhere: "saves you" on one poster, "don't lose" on another. When I see a big percentage, I turn the pack over and read the other side.

qa.q: What did Disha's juice carton say in huge green letters?
qa.a: It said: "90% real fruit!"

qa.q: Why did Disha feel healthy holding one carton but make a face at the other?
qa.a: Disha felt pleased by the first label, which pointed to the good ninety percent, and put off by the second, which pointed to the ten percent syrup, even though both were the same.

qa.q: What habit did Disha pick up after that day at the shop?
qa.a: Whenever a big percentage shows up, Disha turns the pack over and reads the other side, so both the gain and the loss version are visible before choosing.

qa.q: How might Mehak have felt when she turned Disha's carton around?
qa.a: Mehak may have been amused and a little pleased to prove a point, since Disha had just told her to put down a carton that was really the same.

grounding: It shows a student attracted by a figure framed as gain and repelled by the same figure framed as loss, and noticing how often ads use this.

passage: At the university's career fair, two stalls sold the same data-analytics course from rival institutes, at the same fee. The first banner said, in gold: 90% OF OUR STUDENTS GET PLACED! The second, a plain printed sheet, said: 10% of our students were not placed last year. Santosh was already at the gold banner, filling in the form. Himani read both. "Santosh, look. They say the same thing." "No, the second one sounds bad. Ten percent not placed? That's scary." "And ninety percent placed isn't?" Santosh paused, pen hovering. "When you say it like that, they're identical." "The second one is just more honest about who it leaves out," Himani said. Santosh put the pen down and asked both stalls the same question: how many students, and placed where?

qa.q: What did the second stall's sheet say?
qa.a: 10% of our students were not placed last year.

qa.q: Why was Santosh drawn to the gold banner?
qa.a: The placed wording made Santosh feel hopeful and excited, while the not-placed wording of the same figure felt scary.

qa.q: What question did Santosh finally ask, and why is it useful?
qa.a: How many students, and placed where, which turns both wordings into actual numbers that can be compared.

qa.q: How does Himani see the two stalls?
qa.a: Himani sees them as saying the same thing, with the second simply more honest about who it leaves out.

grounding: A student is drawn to a course advertised by its success rate and put off by the same figure stated as a failure rate.

passage:
Hi Salma,
A funny thing happened while I was laptop shopping, and I think you'll enjoy it. Shop A had a huge poster: "SAVE 20%! Festival offer!" I felt this rush, like I'd miss out if I didn't buy right then. Shop B, two doors down, had the same model with a small tag: "Price after festival discount: 80% of MRP." I nearly walked past. It sounded like I was paying almost full price. Then I did the maths on my phone. Exactly the same amount. Same laptop, same price, same warranty. The only difference was that one sentence made me feel like I was winning and the other made me feel like I was losing.
I bought from Shop B, just to prove to myself I could.
Chaitanya

qa.q: What did Shop B's tag say?
qa.a: Price after festival discount: 80% of MRP.

qa.q: How did Shop A's poster make Chaitanya feel?
qa.a: It gave Chaitanya a rush and a fear of missing out, as if buying right then meant winning.

qa.q: What helped Chaitanya see through the wording?
qa.a: Doing the maths on the phone to compare the actual amounts, which showed both offers were identical.

qa.q: What would change if Shop B used Shop A's poster?
qa.a: Shop B would probably draw far more buyers, even though nothing about the laptop or the price changed.

grounding: A student writes about being pulled by a 'save 20%' poster and nearly passing up the same price worded as 80 percent.

passage: Tushar, you know that music app I've been paying for? I signed up because the pop-up said, "Just 99 rupees a month, less than a cup of coffee!" I felt so smart. It sounded tiny. Yesterday I was checking my bank app and saw the yearly total: eleven hundred and eighty-eight rupees. I actually said "what?" out loud in the library. Same thing, right? Ninety-nine times twelve. But one felt like a coffee and the other felt like a pair of shoes. And when the trial ended, the message said, "Don't lose your playlists!", which is why I didn't cancel. Losing felt worse than paying. So now I write every offer three ways: per month, per year, and what I'd lose. Anand's new hobby. Very exciting stuff.

qa.q: What yearly total did Anand see?
qa.a: Eleven hundred and eighty-eight rupees.

qa.q: How did Anand feel on seeing the yearly total?
qa.a: Anand felt shocked, saying "what?" out loud, because the same cost now felt like a pair of shoes instead of a coffee.

qa.q: What habit has Anand started, and why does it help?
qa.a: Writing every offer three ways, per month, per year and what would be lost, so no single wording decides.

qa.q: How might Tushar react to Anand's story?
qa.a: Tushar may laugh but also check Tushar's own subscriptions, seeing how a small monthly figure hides the bigger total.

grounding: A student describes how a monthly price and a 'don't lose your playlists' message steered a choice that the yearly figure would not have.

passage:
Monday. The banner outside the metro station glowed: 80% OF OUR STUDENTS CLEAR THE ENTRANCE! Gautam stopped, took a photo, and booked a free demo class for Saturday before his train came.
Thursday. In the canteen, Arohi slid a flyer across the table. It was from a rival centre and said the same place "fails one in five students, even after a full year." Gautam's stomach dropped. "One in five? That's terrible." He cancelled the Saturday demo on the spot.
The next Monday. Walking past the banner again, he did the maths in his head and stopped dead. One in five was twenty percent. Eighty clear, twenty don't. The banner and the flyer said exactly the same thing. He rebooked the demo, and at the desk he asked a new question: "How many students joined last year, and how many cleared?"

qa.q: What did the banner outside the metro station say?
qa.a: 80% OF OUR STUDENTS CLEAR THE ENTRANCE!

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when he read Arohi's flyer?
qa.a: He felt alarmed and put off, his stomach dropping at "one in five" failing, though it was the same figure as the banner.

qa.q: What question helps Gautam see past the packaging, and why?
qa.a: Asking how many joined and how many cleared gives real counts, so neither the gain wording nor the loss wording can steer him.

qa.q: How might the makers of the banner and the flyer see Gautam?
qa.a: Both seem to count on him reacting to wording: the banner wants him hopeful, the rival flyer wants him scared, using one number.

grounding: Shows a student drawn in by an '80% clear' banner and put off by 'one in five fail', then seeing they state the same figure.

passage: Vandana, you're showing me this phone screen that says "Save today only," and your eyes are shining. Let me tell you something from my college days in Goa, child. Two shops near our hostel sold the same bicycle. The shop by the church had a board: STUDENTS SAVE 400 RUPEES! I, Elizabeth, the careful one, almost ran inside. The shop by the bus stand had a board: NON-STUDENTS PAY 400 EXTRA. That one made me cross. Who likes being told they pay extra? I walked out of it in a huff. A week later my roommate, who had bought hers at the bus stand shop, put her receipt beside mine. Same bicycle, same student price, to the rupee. I had loved one board and hated the other for saying one thing. Now when a number makes me feel something, I turn it around first.

qa.q: What did the board at the shop by the church say?
qa.a: STUDENTS SAVE 400 RUPEES!

qa.q: Why did the second shop's board make Elizabeth cross?
qa.a: Being told someone pays extra felt like a penalty, so Elizabeth felt annoyed, even though a student paid the same price there.

qa.q: Which moment in the story showed Elizabeth what had happened?
qa.a: When the roommate put both receipts side by side with the same price, Elizabeth saw the reaction had been to the wording, not the deal.

qa.q: How might the roommate have seen Elizabeth walking out of the second shop?
qa.a: The roommate may have found it odd or a little funny, since that shop gave her exactly the same student price.

grounding: An elder recalls being drawn to 'students save' and put off by 'non-students pay extra', though both boards gave the same price.

passage: The phone-accessory stall at the Diwali market was shutting in ten minutes, and the loudspeaker next door was blaring songs. Pooja held up a clear case. Pooja put the case down as if it were hot. "One in ten? Forget it." The stall owner was already pulling the shutter halfway down. Kiran laughed. "It's the same test, Pooja. passage:
Alka had been looking at coaching centres for the bank exams for a week in Kanpur. One poster outside the station said: "80% of our students clear the exam!" She felt a rush of hope and took a photo.

The next centre's poster said: "Only 20% of our students fail to clear." Alka felt a small chill. Twenty percent fail? She walked past it quickly.

At home, she told her friend Saurabh, "The first one sounds so much better."

Saurabh looked at both photos. "Alka, they're the same number. Eighty clear, twenty don't."

She looked again. He was right. The first made her feel hopeful; the second made her feel afraid. Nothing had changed except the words.

"And they don't say how many students, or what 'clear' means," Saurabh added.

Alka deleted both photos and wrote down three questions to ask each centre in person.

qa.q: What did the first poster say?
qa.a: 80% of our students clear the exam!

qa.q: How did the second poster make Alka feel?
qa.a: The second poster made Alka feel a small chill of fear, because "20% fail" sounded worse even though it was the same figure.

qa.q: What did Alka decide to do instead of trusting the posters?
qa.a: Alka wrote three questions to ask each centre in person, so she could judge on facts, not wording.

qa.q: How does Saurabh see the posters?
qa.a: Saurabh sees both as the same figure dressed differently, and also notices what the posters leave out.

grounding: A student feels drawn to an "80% clear" poster and put off by "20% fail", though the figures are identical.

passage:
"Nilesh, look at this laptop deal! Twenty percent off!"

"Where, Mehak?"

"This shop. And the other shop says, 'Pay only eighty percent of the price.'"

"And?"

"The first one feels like a steal. The second feels like I'm still paying a lot."

"Mehak. Twenty off is paying eighty."

"...Oh."

"And check the original price. The first shop's laptop might be more expensive to start with."

Mehak scrolled. The first shop's original price was higher. After the discount, it cost more than the second shop's.

"I nearly bought the more expensive one because of the word 'off'."

"That's exactly what they want."

"So how do I not fall for it?"

"Look at the final price. Ignore how they say it."

Mehak wrote both final prices on her hand, side by side.

qa.q: What did the second shop's offer say?
qa.a: Pay only eighty percent of the price.

qa.q: Why did the first deal feel better to Mehak?
qa.a: Mehak felt excited because "twenty percent off" sounded like a gain, while "pay eighty percent" sounded like still paying a lot.

qa.q: What did Nilesh suggest, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Nilesh suggested looking only at the final price, which removes the effect of the wording.

qa.q: How might the shops see buyers like Mehak?
qa.a: The shops count on buyers reacting to the word "off" rather than checking the final price.

grounding: A student is drawn to "twenty percent off" and put off by "pay eighty percent", until a friend points to the final price.

passage:
I'm Lokesh. Last month I nearly signed up for a food delivery subscription because of one sentence.

The ad said: "90% of subscribers keep their plan after the first month!" I felt reassured. Sounds like people love it, I thought.

Then my friend Aparna showed me another ad for the same service, from a different month: "1 in 10 subscribers cancels after the first month." That felt worrying. People cancel?

We laughed when we realised. Ninety percent stay. One in ten leave. Exactly the same.

What bothered me was how differently I'd reacted. The first made me want to sign up. The second made me hesitate. Nothing about the service had changed.

Aparna said, "And they didn't say why the one in ten left."

Now when I see an offer, I flip it in my head. If it says 90% stay, I say 10% leave, and see how I feel both ways.

qa.q: What did the first ad say?
qa.a: 90% of subscribers keep their plan after the first month!

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel reading the two ads?
qa.a: Lokesh felt reassured by "90% keep" and worried by "1 in 10 cancels", even though they meant the same thing.

qa.q: What habit did Lokesh develop, and why does it help?
qa.a: Lokesh flips each claim into its opposite wording to see both feelings, which weakens the pull of the advert's chosen frame.

qa.q: How does Aparna seem to see the ads?
qa.a: Aparna sees through the wording and asks what's missing, like why the one in ten left.

grounding: A student is drawn to an ad framed as ninety percent staying and put off by one in ten cancelling, and learns to flip claims.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Diwali admissions fair, Block C
Amandeep came to my table holding a glossy flyer from a coaching centre for postgraduate entrance exams: "80% of our students reach their target score!" Amandeep was glowing, already asking me about the festive discount. Samir, standing just behind, read the same flyer aloud and said, "So one in five doesn't. That's a lot of people." I watched Amandeep's face drop. The flyer went down on my table as if it were hot. Same flyer, same number, two opposite moods in thirty seconds. I didn't tell either of them which reading was right. I wrote both sentences on a sheet, added "Out of how many students, and what target?", and asked Amandeep to bring those answers back before paying anything. Amandeep tucked the sheet inside the flyer and said, "I'll call them tomorrow."

qa.q: What did the flyer promise?
qa.a: "80% of our students reach their target score!"

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling when Samir said one in five doesn't?
qa.a: Amandeep went from excited to deflated and uneasy, because the same number suddenly sounded like a chance of failing.

qa.q: What did the counsellor ask Amandeep to find out, and why does it help?
qa.a: Out of how many students, and what target, because plain numbers and clear details cut through the flyer's wording in either direction.

qa.q: How does Samir see the same flyer?
qa.a: Samir reads it as a warning, focusing on the one in five who miss the target, which shows how one fact can be framed as a loss.

grounding: Shows a student drawn to an offer framed as a success rate and put off when the same figure is phrased as a failure rate.
